Cliff-Top Riding: Where Road Meets Sea

There's something primal about riding a motorcycle along a cliff edge with the sea hundreds of feet below. The combination of height, exposure, and ocean views creates a riding experience that's both thrilling and meditative. Britain's coastline delivers this in abundance.

North Cornwall Coast (B3306 and Beyond)

The north Cornish coast from St Ives to Land's End is UK cliff-top riding at its finest. The B3306 winds through old tin mining villages perched above dramatic cliffs, past abandoned engine houses silhouetted against the Atlantic.

  • Distance: 20 miles
  • Highlights: Zennor, Botallack Mine, Sennen Cove, Cape Cornwall
  • Character: Narrow, twisting, with stone walls on both sides and the ocean beyond

Pembrokeshire Coast Road

The B4327 and minor roads through Pembrokeshire trace the coastline of this Welsh peninsula through some of the UK's most dramatic coastal scenery. The cliffs at Stack Rocks and the Green Bridge of Wales are geological wonders.

  • Distance: 40 miles (Tenby to St David's via coast roads)
  • Highlights: Barafundle Bay, Broad Haven, Whitesands Bay, St Govan's Chapel

North Devon and Exmoor Coast

The A39 between Lynton and Porlock climbs along England's highest sea cliffs, with the road carved into the hillside above the Bristol Channel. Porlock Hill — a 1-in-4 descent — is infamous among motorcyclists.

Jurassic Coast, Dorset

The B3157 from Weymouth to Bridport runs along the top of Chesil Beach before climbing to clifftop level. The views across Lyme Bay are stunning, and the geology — 185 million years of earth history — is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

Northumberland Coast

The B1340 from Alnmouth to Bamburgh follows the Northumberland coastline past mile upon mile of golden sand, with the Farne Islands visible offshore. Less dramatic than Cornwall's cliffs but more atmospheric — especially with the silhouette of Bamburgh Castle growing larger as you approach.

East Lothian Coast, Scotland

The A198 from Musselburgh to North Berwick follows the south shore of the Firth of Forth past volcanic headlands, sandy beaches, and the dramatic Bass Rock — the world's largest gannet colony.

Northwest Highlands Coast

The single-track roads of Wester Ross and Sutherland offer some of the most dramatic coastal riding in Europe. The road from Durness to Ullapool, part of the NC500, clings to the coast with views across to offshore islands and sea stacks.

Coastal cliff-top roads demand attention. Wind gusts near cliff edges can be sudden and powerful. Keep a firm grip on the bars and be ready for crosswinds, especially on exposed headlands. The views are distracting — save your looking for when you stop.

Safety on Coastal Roads

  • Wind: Coastal roads are exposed to strong winds. On gusty days, reduce speed and keep a firm grip.
  • Salt spray: Coastal moisture is corrosive. Wash your bike after coastal riding to protect metalwork and chain.
  • Visibility: Sea fog (haar) can roll in rapidly on the east coast. Carry a clear visor.
  • Narrow roads: Many coastal roads are single-track with passing places. Be prepared for oncoming traffic, especially campervans in summer.

Best Time for Coastal Riding

Coastal rides are spectacular year-round, but spring and autumn offer the best combination of clear light, dramatic skies, and quiet roads. Summer brings the most reliable weather but also the most traffic. Winter storms create the most dramatic seas but demand serious weatherproofing.

Britain's coastline is 19,491 miles long. You could spend a lifetime exploring it by motorcycle and never run out of new cliff-top roads to discover.

Practical Information

Northumberland is large and sparsely populated. Fuel is available in Alnwick, Rothbury, Hexham, Berwick-upon-Tweed, and Wooler, but distances between stations can be significant in the Cheviots and border areas. Accommodation ranges from wild camping (discreetly tolerated in remote areas) to excellent country house B&Bs. The Lord Crewe Arms in Blanchland, a 12th-century former abbey, is a memorable overnight stop. The Pheasant Inn at Stannersburn, near Kielder, serves locally sourced food in a remote border setting. And the Jolly Fisherman in Craster serves the best crab sandwiches in England — made with locally caught crabs landed at the harbour steps away from the pub doorstep.
keyTakeaways: The B3306 from St Ives to Land's End is UK clifftop riding at its finest, past old tin mines above the Atlantic.
The A39 between Lynton and Porlock climbs England's highest sea cliffs, including the infamous 1-in-4 Porlock Hill.
Dorset's B3157 along the Jurassic Coast runs above Chesil Beach with UNESCO-listed geology.
Coastal roads are exposed to sudden crosswinds, so keep a firm grip and save the views for stops.
Salt spray is corrosive, so wash your bike after coastal riding to protect the chain and metalwork.

faq.q: How dangerous are crosswinds on clifftop roads?
faq.a: Sudden gusts near exposed headlands can shove a bike across its lane, so treat wind as a genuine hazard. On blustery days reduce speed, grip the tank with your knees, and keep a relaxed but firm hold on the bars. Be especially alert where the road emerges from shelter onto open cliff, and where gaps in walls or hedges funnel the wind.

faq.q: When is the best time of year for coastal cliff riding?
faq.a: Spring and autumn offer the best mix of clear light, dramatic skies, and quiet roads. Summer brings the most reliable weather but also the heaviest traffic, particularly campervans on narrow Cornish and Pembrokeshire lanes. Winter delivers the most theatrical seas but demands serious weatherproofing and awareness of exposed, wind-battered sections.

faq.q: Do I need to worry about sea fog?
faq.a: Yes, particularly on the east coast where haar can roll in rapidly and cut visibility to metres. Carry a clear visor rather than a tinted one, slow right down, and use dipped headlights when fog arrives. On the Northumberland and East Lothian coasts fog can appear even on a warm day, so do not be caught out by a bright morning.

faq.q: Should I clean my bike after a coastal ride?
faq.a: Definitely. Salt-laden air and spray are highly corrosive and attack the chain, fasteners, and any exposed metal. Rinse the bike thoroughly after a day near the sea, dry it, and re-lubricate the chain. Regular attention after coastal touring prevents the creeping corrosion that otherwise shortens the life of components and dulls finishes.

faq.q: Are these roads suitable for large touring bikes?
faq.a: The open stretches such as the A39 and A198 handle any machine well. The narrow, walled Cornish lanes of the B3306 and the single-track Highland coast roads are tighter and demand more care with a wide, heavy bike, especially when meeting oncoming traffic in passing places. Ride within your comfort and be ready to give way courteously.
